en: The Ritual for the Practice of the Dharani of the Great Compassionate Heart of the Thousand Hands and Eyes,
compiled by the Shramana Zhili of Sizhou.
Having been fortunate enough to recite this great dharani from my early childhood, I have nonetheless not yet mastered its retention.
Later, he studied the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school,
investigating their scriptural texts.
The ritual procedures for the practice of contemplative wisdom are sufficient for practical application;
therefore, I have set them forth here in brief, which can truly serve as a standard for oneself.
Nevertheless, these ritual procedures were established by the wise.
In total there are four kinds. What are the four?
The first is called constant sitting.
The first is the *Ekavyūha-samādhi* from the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
The second is called the "Constant Practice," which is the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* (Banzhou jing) of the Buddha’s standing meditation.
The third is called "half-walking and half-sitting," which refers to the two sutras, the Vaipulya and the Lotus Sutra;
it involves the practice of the two samādhis of Samantabhadra while baring one shoulder.
The fourth is neither walking nor sitting.
This involves relying on various methods of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) as well as practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) throughout the states of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
This is collectively termed the Samādhi of Following One’s Own Intent.
According to this sutra, one is not restricted to sitting exclusively; rather, there are only the practices of walking and that which is half-and-half [of walking and sitting].
Nor is it a matter of indulging the three natures;
rather, one should remain vigilant within them and recite and maintain the practice according to the Dharma for twenty-one days.
This is the method of practicing according to the sutras as found in the *Sui-zi-i* (Following One’s Own Intent).
Now, ten points are set forth from this fundamental sūtra:
first, adorning the site of enlightenment; second, purifying the three karmas;
third, delimiting the boundary; and fourth, practicing offerings.
Five: Invoking the Triple Gem and the various devas; Six: Praising and expressing sincerity;
Seven: Prostrating; Eight: Making vows and reciting mantras;
Nine: Repenting; Ten: Cultivating contemplative practice.
Furthermore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* is appended as a supplement to the visualization;
it is placed beneath the ritual procedures so that those who practice may avoid having to consult other texts.
First, adorning the site of enlightenment (*maṇḍala*):
The Sūtra says, "Dwell in a pure chamber, suspend banners, and light lamps;
offer incense, flowers, food, and drink as offerings."
The *Bai lu* (Record of a Hundred [Texts]) on the Ritual for Invoking Avalokiteśvara states:
"One should solemnly adorn the ritual site (*maṇḍala*),
smear the ground with fragrant mud, and suspend various banners and canopies."
The Buddha image should be installed facing south;
the Avalokiteśvara image should be installed separately facing east.
Now, one must install an image of Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara.
Or forty hands. If such an image does not exist,
one should simply [pray] before an image with six or four hands.
Alternatively, it may consist solely of the form and appearance of Avalokiteśvara;
furthermore, there is no harm in additionally installing images of Śākyamuni, Śrīkṣetra (Śrī-Ābhāsvara), and others.
The practitioner should have at least ten people.
One should sit on the ground facing west;
if the ground is low or damp, one should place a low-legged bed.
One should offer worship with all one's strength every day.
If one cannot provide [offerings], there must still be some giving on the first day.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says:
"Although one's heart and mouth may be sincere, one must rely on merit to assist."
If one practices day after day, the merit increases ever further.
Fearing that one's strength may not suffice, one may choose to begin from the first day;
however, one must first set aside one's resources to demonstrate total dedication.
The Sūtra says:
"If there are sentient beings who seek the fulfillment of their vows in the present life,
they should maintain the pure observance of the fast and precepts for twenty-one days."
Reciting this dhāraṇī will surely fulfill one's aspirations.
According to this practice, one must take twenty-one days as a single session;
it must by no means be reduced.
Prior to the formal cultivation of the Lotus Samādhi,
one should practice the preparatory methods for one seven-day period,
ensuring that both the ritual procedures and the contemplation of principle are thoroughly mastered.
Furthermore, one should seek their protection so as to be free from obstacles.
Second, purifying the three karmas. As the Sūtra says:
Those who recite this divine mantra shall give rise to the vast bodhicitta and vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Maintaining the fast and precepts, dwell in a quiet chamber;
having bathed for purification, put on clean garments;
restrain the mind to a single point and allow no other distractions.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* states:
"When first entering the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*),
one should bathe with fragrant water and don clean, pure garments."
If it is the great robe (saṃghāṭī) or various newly dyed garments,
or if there are no new ones,
one should take the most excellent among one's already possessed robes.
One should consider this as the robe for entering the maṇḍala.
Thereafter, if one exits the maṇḍala and arrives at an impure place,
one should remove the pure robe and put on the impure robe.
When the task to be performed is completed, one should bathe and put on one's original pure robes.
Entering the *maṇḍala* to perform the ritual, all the aforementioned procedures are from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Even if it lasts for an entire day, one must not fall into impurity at all.
One must also bathe once;
throughout the entire period, one must remain focused and refrain from all mixed speech,
as well as from all forms of social interaction, greetings, and inquiries.
Throughout the entire course of one's life, one should rely on the sutras to cultivate contemplation,
never allowing for even a single moment of thought regarding worldly affairs.
Even when attending to the necessities of defecation, urination, eating, or drinking, one must maintain focused mindfulness and protection.
Do not allow them to be lost or scattered.
Once the task is completed, enter the ritual arena immediately; do not delay by making excuses.
In brief, the body concerns what is permitted and what is prohibited;
the mouth concerns speech and silence;
and the mind concerns cessation and contemplation.
The practitioner must consult and receive instruction from a virtuous teacher;
once they have understood this, they may put it into practice.
Be careful not to act on your own authority.

Third, the Delimitation of the Boundary (*Sīmābandha*). On the first day of the construction, before performing prostrations, the practitioner should duly delimit the boundary around the site of practice according to the Dharma.
As the Sūtra says:
As for the method of establishing the boundary:
take a blade, recite the mantra over it twenty-one times,
and draw a line on the ground to form the boundary.
Alternatively, take pure water and recite the mantra over it twenty-one times,
then scatter it in the four directions to establish a boundary.
Or, take white mustard seeds and recite the mantra over them twenty-one times.
One may establish the boundary by casting [the ashes] in the four directions;
or one may establish the boundary wherever the mind reaches;
or one may take pure ashes, recite the mantra twenty-one times over them, and thereby establish the boundary.
Alternatively, one may recite a mantra over five-colored threads twenty-one times and encircle the four sides to establish a boundary; this will be effective for all.
If one can maintain the practice according to the Dharma, the fruit will naturally be attained, as the Sūtra says:
All may practice according to their convenience.
Fourth, the cultivation of offerings: the practitioner, having performed the ritual demarcation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) according to the dharma...
Upon arriving before the Thousand-Eyed Image,
first spread out your sitting mat and stand leaning against it;
you should then bring to mind all the Triple Gem.
As for the sentient beings of the dharma-realm,
they are non-dual and indistinguishable from my own body and mind.
While the Buddhas have already awakened to this, sentient beings remain deluded.
In order to overturn the delusions and obstacles of sentient beings,
I pay homage and serve the Triple Gem.
Having formed this thought, one should recite aloud:
With all reverence and single-minded devotion,
having performed one prostration to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions:
They burned incense and scattered flowers.
The leader addressed the assembly, saying: "Each of you should kneel on your right knees and reverently hold incense and flowers to make offerings according to the Dharma.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the worlds of the ten directions."
Each and every buddha-field is adorned with immeasurable fragrances;
having fully perfected the bodhisattva path and attained the fragrance of a Tathāgata, one should form this thought:
"May these my fragrant flowers pervade the ten directions."
He perceives it as a subtle and wondrous pavilion of light,
with celestial music and divine precious incense,
celestial delicacies and divine precious garments.
The inconceivable dust of the sublime Dharma:
from each and every particle of dust emerge all particles of dust;
from each and every particle of dust emerge all dharmas.
Rotating without obstruction, they mutually adorn one another,
reaching everywhere before the Triple Gem in the ten directions and throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.
In each and every instance, my own body performs offerings,
pervading the entire dharma realm; in each and every place,
they are without confusion and without obstruction.
Performing buddha-works throughout the limits of the future,
universally perfuming all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm;
through this perfuming, all shall give rise to the bodhicitta.
Together enter the non-arising [state] and realize the Buddha-wisdom.
Having thus visualized and offered these, all remain reverently attentive.
Fifth, invite the Triple Gem and the celestial practitioners, directing the mind accordingly.
Having made universal offerings,
kneel on your right knee and burn incense;
you should then keep the Triple Gem in mind.
Although he is pure through being free from all obscurations,
he nonetheless possesses a compassion identical in essence [to his own] that protects and mindfuly attends to all classes of beings.
If one can invoke [the deity] through the three karmas of body, speech,
and mind, they will surely come even if not invited;
they shall uproot suffering and bestow happiness.
However, one must with utmost sincerity and diligent devotion make three requests for each position;
there will certainly be a responsive descent. Chant:
"With a single mind, we respectfully invite."
Homage to the World-Honored One, Śākyamuni, our Original Teacher.
With single-minded devotion, we respectfully entreat you.
Homage to the World-Honored One, Amitābha, of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge and entreat:
Homage to the World-Honored One, King of a Thousand Rays, Abiding in Tranquility, of the past immeasurable billions of kalpas.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge and entreat.
Homage to the ninety-nine billion *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the past.
With single-minded devotion, we extend our invitation.
Homage to the World-Honored One, Right Dharma-Light, of immeasurable kalpas past.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in and entreat all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions.
With single-minded devotion, we take refuge in and entreat them.
Homage to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa and to all the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion, we extend our invitation.
Homage to the Great Dharani of the Wondrous Phrases of the Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Great Compassionate Mind. The thought-cloud [of this dharani] is as follows:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is like space and cannot be seen.
The eternally abiding Dharma Jewel is inconceivable;
I now entreat you with my three karmas according to the Dharma.
I only pray that you will manifest yourself and accept this offering.
The subsequent stages are likewise.
With single-minded devotion, one should offer this invocation:
"Homage to all the dhāraṇīs spoken by Avalokiteśvara."
And all the honored Dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time—single-mindedly I invoke you.
Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent One with a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes; contemplate him as being like a Buddha.
Simply change it to read: "The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara is also like this.

Homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dhāraṇīśvara-rāja.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in and entreat: Namo to the Bodhisattva Sunlight and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Moonlight.
With single-minded devotion,

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja,

The Bodhisattva Mahāsaṃbhava and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnagarbha reverently entreated him with single-minded devotion.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Guṇakośa,
the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, and the Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in and entreat Maitreya Bodhisattva and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, with single-minded devotion, makes this invocation:
Homage to all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
With single-minded devotion,
we take refuge in and entreat Mahākāśyapa and the immeasurable,
innumerable assembly of great śrāvaka monks.
With single-minded devotion,
we offer our invocation to the Brahmā-putra gods Śaṅkha and Vāmadeva,
and to the Four World-Protecting Kings.
The eight classes of devas and nāgas, the goddess Tóngmù,
the spirits of space,
and the spirits of rivers and seas.
The deity of springs and sources;
the deity of rivers and marshes;
the deity of medicinal herbs, trees, and forests.
The deity of the dwelling,
the deity of water, the deity of fire,
the deity of wind, and the deity of earth.
The mountain deities, earth deities, palace deities,
and those who protect and uphold the dhāraṇīs.
All devas, nāgas, spirits, and their respective retinues, we pray only that Śākyamuni, the Original Teacher; Amitābha, the Compassionate Father;
and Tathāgata King of a Thousand Rays Abiding in Tranquility—[will grant us your protection].
All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
without departing from the fundamental limit, descend upon this site of enlightenment to bear witness to my practice of the Dharma through their impartial compassion.
With a vast, perfect, and unimpeded heart of great compassion,
you who manifest the secret essentials of dhāraṇī at this site of enlightenment,
please accept my offerings.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara of a Thousand Hands and a Thousand Eyes,
by the power of his original vow, came before me;
through the empowerment of his divine mantra, the three obstacles were instantly eliminated.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, such as the Dhāraṇī King Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
and the great Śrāvakas, such as Mahākāśyapa,
all moved by compassion and descended together at the same time.
May Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the eight classes of devas come at my request;
may they steadfastly guard the site of practice and protect those who uphold the mantra.
May all demonic obstacles be dispelled and auspiciousness be manifested, so that my practice shall not deviate from its original vow.
Sixth, the expression of praise: although this sūtra does not contain verses of praise, I offer these words of sincere homage.
I wished to cite other sutras,
but fearing that they might slightly differ from the essence of the mantra and its manifestations,
I have instead briefly composed this praise based upon the sutra itself.
Homage to the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa of the past.
To the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara appearing before us,
who has perfected wondrous merit and is endowed with great compassion.
Within a single body and mind, he manifests a thousand hands and eyes;
illuminating and perceiving the Dharma-realm, he protects and sustains sentient beings,
causing them to give rise to the vast Bodhicitta.
By upholding this perfected divine mantra,
one shall forever leave the evil realms behind and be reborn before the Buddha;
even the grave transgressions of the Avīci Hell and the malignant diseases that afflict the body shall be eliminated.
May none be left unable to receive rescue or relief, but may all afflictions be eliminated.
May whatever vows and aspirations one seeks and prays for in this present life be fully realized, without any doubt.
It enables one to swiftly attain the three vehicles and quickly ascend to the stage of Buddhahood;
the power of its majestic spiritual authority is beyond the reach of praise.
Therefore, with single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage;
I set forth my sincere intentions and speak according to the reality of my own intellectual capacity.
However, the matters sought after must not increase birth and death; as for the mind that is exercised,
it must be directed accordingly.
One must benefit the multitudes;
only through single-minded diligence can there be spiritual resonance.
Be careful not to treat this lightly.
One who performs the sevenfold prostration should keep in mind that the Three Jewels are the embodiment of unconditioned compassion,
constantly desiring to rescue and deliver all sentient beings.
It is simply because they lack the karmic affinity that [the response] cannot arise.
Since I have entreated you repeatedly,
even if it is not witnessed by the eyes, the spiritual response will surely not be in vain.
Therefore, one must form the thought of having already brought [the deities] down, burn various sublime incenses,
and prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to the Triple Gem as previously invoked.
One need not pay homage to the various devas and spirits. However,
upon reaching the Great Compassionate Heart Mantra and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
one must perform three prostrations for each.
Since this person is the presiding master of the *dharma-cakra*, they proclaim:
"With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Bhagavān, as well as the various positions of the Triple Gem as requested previously."
In all cases, one must prostrate with the five limbs touching the ground and diligently perform the profound rites of reverence.
When bowing to the Buddha, one should contemplate thus:
"The nature of both the one who bows and the object of veneration is empty and quiescent."
The mutual resonance of the Way is inconceivable.

Visualizing my own form before the Jewel of the Dharma, I single-mindedly take refuge and pay homage according to the Dharma.
My homage to the Saṅgha follows the same procedure as that for the Buddha,
with the sole modification that "Bodhisattvas" and so forth are substituted.
One should simply pay obeisance to Avalokiteśvara,

Eighth, making vows and upholding mantras.
The Sūtra states: "If there be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās..."
Whether a boy or a girl who wishes to recite and uphold [this],

First, you should make such a vow as this from me.
This vow is profoundly deep and encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate;
it is only through the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai that one can reach its furthest limits.
Now, I shall briefly provide a summary based on one school of thought, so that practitioners may have a point of orientation for their minds.
This vow consists of two sections; the first ten vows clarify the methods for accomplishment, specifically the excellence of rebirth.
The latter six vows clarify the method of eradication, which for the time being destroys evil;
however, this is based on the recitation of the mantra.
One attains the benefits of the four fruits and the ten stages (*bhūmi*),
as manifested in the Vaipulya section. This vow is intended for Bodhisattvas of the four teachings,
while incidentally encompassing the two vehicles (*yāna*) of the two [lower] teachings.
There is also compassion that takes phenomena as its object,

As for practitioners today:

Therefore, Jingxi said:

yet their primary intent lies solely in the *amṛta* (the 'Ghee' stage)."
The sixteen vows must be interpreted according to the meaning of the revealed, perfect teaching (*vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).
In the first ten vows, all refer to "Namo to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara.
*Namo* is translated as "taking refuge" and also means "deliver me."
They also place their faith and follow those who possess great compassion;
for because these bodhisattvas extract the pain of others' hearts with such gravity,

furthermore, this vow is itself the power and function of the original nature.
As Aśvaghoṣa said:
Giving rise to faith within one's own mind, one returns to place faith in one's own mind.
This sutra states:

I shall now explain these ten vows through two meanings:
first, by correlating them with the Four Great Vows found in various sutras;
second, by correlating them with the Ten Modes of Practice (Shichō) of our own school.
Now, the Four Great Vows arise based upon the Four Noble Truths.
As for the Four Noble Truths, the first two demonstrate the causes and effects of suffering in the mundane world,
while the latter two demonstrate the causes and effects of bliss in the supramundane realm.
All bodhisattvas, wishing to uproot this suffering and wishing to bestow this happiness,
therefore rely upon them to establish the four vows.
Based on the Truth of Suffering, it is established that "I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
Based on the Truth of Origination, it is established that "I vow to sever innumerable afflictions.
Based on the Truth of the Path, it is established that "I vow to know inexhaustible Dharma gates."
Based on the Truth of Cessation, it is established that "I vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way.
However, these current ten vows prioritize the eradication of the causes of suffering in the world.
Therefore, while the sequence differs slightly from that of the four vows,
they all function in pairs to support one another;
for it is by knowing the Dharma through the eye that one brings sentient beings across by means of wisdom.
Just as one must rely on a boat of skillful means to cross the sea,
and can rely on a mountain dwelling to take up residence,
the first two [truths] are established based on the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
First, I vow to know that all phenomena of affliction are themselves the Dharma-realm;
next, I vow to attain this perfectly pure eye of wisdom.
Because this wisdom cannot be known by anything other than itself,
the third and fourth reliances are established based on the Truth of Suffering.
First, one vows to deliver all sentient beings who are submerged in the cycle of existence.
Next, one vows to quickly attain the internal skillful means (*adhyātma-upāya*),
for without these skillful means, the salvation of sentient beings cannot be universal.
The [stages] five, six, seven, and eight are established based on the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Although the Path consists of myriad practices, they are not outside the three trainings.
Now, first one seeks the wisdom of *prajñā*, which is the training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*).
Next, one vows that this wisdom shall be perfected so as to transcend the ocean of suffering of the two deaths.
Next, one seeks the supramundane, supreme morality and concentration;
subsequently, one vows that the merits of these two trainings shall be perfected so as to enter the three virtues.
The three trainings of nirvana constitute the beginning of the Truth of the Path.
Transcending suffering and realizing cessation marks the conclusion of the Truth of the Path.
The ninety [dharmas] are established based on the Truth of Cessation; first, one seeks the unconditioned dharma to settle the mind therein.
Then delusion will be extinguished and conditioned activity will cease;
subsequently, one’s vows will merge with the Dharma-nature,
and the primordial pure body will be restored.
Thus, they are ultimately and eternally quiescent; even if one makes hundreds or thousands of vows, how could they possibly transcend the Four Great Vows?
How much less so these ten?
Furthermore, a vow that does not rely upon the Truths is called a deluded vow.
Although they do not exceed four,
now, because Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom is skillful and his compassion is profound,
these four are expanded into ten.

for from the beginning to the end, everything is made clearly manifest.

"From the very first moment of the mind, one universally encompasses the contemplation of delusions as the dharma-realm."
That delusion itself becomes wisdom and that birth itself becomes cessation;
this is called the perfection of the four vows.
Furthermore, one realizes the first two vows.
It uproots the suffering of the nature-endowed virtues;
the latter two vows bestow the bliss of the nature-endowed virtues.
These are the suffering and bliss of the nature.

Second, regarding the explanation according to our own school’s ten stages of practice (daśayāna):
The Sage’s intention is manifold; let us provide two interpretations.
By examining the beginning and end of the sutra and verifying the latter against the former, we know that this is the fulfillment of the vow to establish the Ten Dharma-Vehicles.
What is this? Before reciting the mantra, one is instructed to make ten vows;
upon finishing the recitation of the mantra, the characteristics of the mantra are revealed, consisting of nine phrases together with the mantra itself.
The substance consists of ten dharmas,

It will be explained later in the section on contemplative practice:
as for the ten vehicles,
the first is the contemplation of the inconceivable realm.
Second, generating the bodhicitta;
third, skillfully establishing śamatha and vipaśyanā;
fourth, the universal penetration of dharmas.
1. The five consciousnesses are characterized by their penetration and obstruction; 2. the six [faculties] are the path of adaptation; 3.
the antidotes assist in opening [the way].
Eighth, knowing the sequence of stages;
ninth, patient endurance;
tenth, being free from attachment to the dharmas that accord with the path.
The ten vows correspond to this;
they differ only in their sequence.
Those [vows] arise based on the objective realm.
This constitutes the cultivation of contemplation based on the object;
each has its own specific intent. First, one understands all phenomena as being like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
This reveals the inconceivable realm.
If it were not "the three thousand in a single thought-moment," how could it encompass all things?
Second is the vow for the eye of wisdom:
it is the fulfillment of cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) to achieve the wisdom of the Buddha-eye.
For without this eye-wisdom, the wondrous realm would not be revealed.
Third, it is the stage of generating the bodhicitta that fulfills all vows for all sentient beings;
because it manifests only from the first bhūmi (Prathamabhūmi) onwards, it provides salvation through unconditional compassion.
The fourth is the vow of skillful means;
it accomplishes the breaking of pervasiveness. Once the three delusions have been broken, [the next stage follows].
Only then can one spontaneously and universally eradicate [delusions];
this is precisely the skillful means for delivering sentient beings.
It is through this that the Bodhisattva destroys afflictions.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings, there is the fifth vow: the boat of prajñā.
It is like having a boat upon the water to discern what is passable and what is obstructed.
This means that what was previously obstructed is now made permeable.
Sixth is the "Vow to Cross the Sea of Suffering," which constitutes the Chapter on Attaining the Way.
Because there is no path of non-action that can transcend the ocean of the two deaths,
the seventh— precepts, concentration, the path, and vows—
constitutes the fulfillment of the aids to the path.
One cultivates the precepts and meditative concentration with a mind of non-action,
for this is most capable of subduing evil.
Eighth is the vow to ascend the mountain of nirvana.
This refers to knowing the sequence of stages.
A mountain must be ascended from the bottom upward;
although one contemplates that phenomena are identical to principle, the path does not proceed by leaping over the steps. Therefore, [the stages must be followed].
The ninth assembly is the relinquishing of vows for the sake of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
this constitutes the practice of patience (*kṣānti*).
It is called "relinquishing" because one abandons the multitude [of vows] in order to swiftly realize the unconditioned.
This practice is not exclusive;
the same applies to the initial stages and the higher realms.
Even when gods and nāgas pay him homage, he does not take pleasure in it.
This is precisely an example of that.
The tenth is the vow for the Dharmatā-kāya,
which is free from attachment to dharmas.
Not stagnating in what merely resembles understanding, one accords with the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*).
Thus, according to the text, the two pairs are mutually established:
the illumination of objects arises through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
One eradicates delusions through the power of cultivation;
only after first discerning what is obstructed and what is permeable does one cultivate the factors of enlightenment.
Without the efficacy of antidotes, how could there be successive stages?
If one does not practice patient endurance,
there would be no semblance of craving from which to be liberated.
This is the method of contemplation.
Cultivation exists in the stage of names; accomplishment occurs in the five grades.
A semblance of arousal occurs in the six faculties;
true arousal occurs in the stage of partial realization.
Ultimate mastery lies in wondrous enlightenment.
Those who now establish vows aspire to cultivate the means to enter it and achieve it within this very life.
Whether through a single contemplation or by passing through other states of mind,
one enters into that which resembles the true [state] and thereby reaches the stage of equality and excellence.
Furthermore, one should know these ten dharmas.
Although one discusses cultivation, realization, causes, and effects,
the present single thought-moment is fundamentally and inherently perfected from the beginning.
When cultivation arises entirely from the nature, the cause itself becomes the fruit.
Now I establish these ten vows, directing my mind toward them.
Furthermore, it should be understood that although these ten dharmas were proclaimed by wise ones during the Semblance Age, they remain relevant here.
These are all the essential tenets of the various gradual and sudden sutras;
for apart from these ten, there is no further method of cultivation or realization.
The "Great Vehicle" of the *Lotus Sutra* can be deeply cited as an analogy for this.
Of the six subsequent vows, one generally destroys evil.
Among them, the first three destroy the hells;
specifically, the first two separately destroy the two types of suffering involving swords and fire.
The third [vow] destroys all hells;
the latter three destroy the remaining three destinies.
It should be understood that these six vows are established according to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic remedies).
Therefore, for those in hell, it is called "crushing and withering";
for hungry ghosts, "satiating";
and for asuras, "subduing."
Regarding animals, they are said to possess wisdom.

Because humans possess both the entry into principle and the flourishing of contemplation;
the remaining four [realms] all proceed from counteractive measures,

"All that which is designated as 'self,' though it is what practitioners refer to,

In a single thought-moment, there are a thousand dharmas.

"Yak" (若) is an indeterminate term; it corresponds to the various destinies (*gati*) as their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
All instances of "kō" (向) are explained as meaning "to face" or "to correspond."
The meaning of "as an antidote" is perfectly consistent:
the self-nature of the four destinies serves as the antidote,
while the three obstructions of the four destinies serve as that which is to be countered.
Regarding the statement that "all are self-originated":
the three obstacles are fundamentally empty, yet they exist due to ignorance;
they are treated by means of the Perfect Dharma.
It is called fundamentally empty and harmonious, and is no longer an obstruction;
hence it is said that "it crushes itself," and so forth. Nevertheless, there can still be the distinction of self and other within this capacity for response.
There are three obstacles to be remedied:
one remedies them oneself through the practice of affairs and the contemplation of principle;
others remedy them through debate, supernatural powers, and spiritual responses.
What is this? It is when one personally gives rise to the afflictions of the four realms of existence,
creates the unwholesome karma of the four realms of existence,
and undergoes the suffering of the four realms of existence.
One recites the name and chants the mantra while facing [the image].
One should pray: "May these three obstacles be spontaneously shattered and destroyed.
This is the practice of remedial action (*pratipakṣa*).
If one personally employs the tenfold contemplative wisdom,

This principle is the contemplation that serves as the remedy.
If one’s own contemplative practice is perfected, one can destroy the three obstructions,
manifest the nature of the self, and attain great sovereignty.
Seeing all sentient beings suffering from the four destinies and the three obstacles,

This is precisely responding through the treatment of others.

Now, having established the aforementioned vows in accordance with the Perfect Dharma, they are called "unconditioned vows" (*anabhisaṃskāra-praṇidhāna*), and their merit is vast and immeasurable. One may ask:
what is meant by "perfect understanding" (*pariniṣpanna-adhimukti*) and "perfect cultivation" (*pariniṣpanna-bhāvanā*)?
It may be that one gains benefit; however,
for one who lacks this understanding,
what benefit is there in practice?
Answer: The essence of phenomena is inherently so.
When the sages refer to this "original state" to demonstrate its cultivation, even if one has not yet attained perfect understanding, [the practice will nonetheless be effective].
It is simply that when the conditions are met, benefit is spontaneously obtained;
if one can understand this, its merit is beyond measure,
like a mani jewel.
If a fool obtains it, it is not entirely without benefit;
it merely serves to provide for one garment and one meal.
However, as for one who possesses discernment:
Because one cultivates the ten matters and rains down jewels upon the four continents,
the scripture states: "For those who possess wisdom, insight, and skillful means,

Therefore, the practitioner should personally attend upon a virtuous teacher to study this perfect understanding;
at the moment of establishing their vow, let their mind and speech be as one.
The three obstacles will immediately vanish and the Dharma-body will be swiftly realized. Having briefly understood this principle, one should make this vow.

The sutra says: Having made this vow...

and you should also single-mindedly keep in mind my original teacher,
the Tathāgata Amitābha.

as if one who has encountered fire or drowning were seeking rescue.

if time is somewhat more ample, there is no harm in reciting it many times. After reciting "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" and "Namo Amitābha Buddha," say the following:

if there are sentient beings who recite and uphold this Great Compassionate Divine Mantra..."
If those who recite and uphold this Great Compassion Divine Mantra should fall into the three evil realms, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
If I do not attain rebirth in the lands of all Buddhas,
I vow not to achieve perfect enlightenment.
I shall recite and uphold this Great Compassion Divine Mantra.
If I do not attain immeasurable samādhi and eloquence,
I vow not to achieve perfect enlightenment.
I shall recite and uphold this divine mantra of Great Compassion.
If, within this present life,
all that one seeks is not successfully accomplished,
it cannot be called the Mahākaruṇā-hṛdaya-dhāraṇī.
Having spoken these words,

perfect, and unimpeded great compassionate mind,

The great earth shook in six ways;
celestial flowers rained down in profusion;
and all the Buddhas of the ten directions were filled with joy.
The celestial Māras and non-Buddhist heretics were struck with such terror that their hair stood on end;
the entire assembly attained realization of the fruits,
some attaining the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Some attain the fruit of once-returner,
some attain the fruit of non-returner,
and some attain the fruit of arhatship.
Some attain the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, or even the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Immeasurable sentient beings resolve their minds upon *bodhicitta*.
Ninth, the Confession: When the practitioner has finished reciting the mantra.
One should reflect that all conditions and obstacles arise from past causes;
throughout past and present lives, what evil have sentient beings not committed?
Thus, their burden of transgressions has accumulated.
From lifetime to lifetime we shall encounter one another as enemies, as relatives, as obstacles, and as afflictions.
If we do not repent, there will be no means for liberation, and the Way and its Dharma will not be accomplished.
Therefore, one must lay bare one's heart in lamentation and entreat the Triple Gem to extinguish [these afflictions] for me.
As the Sūtra says:
"For the sake of all sentient beings."
I repent for the sins of my past karma,
and I also personally repent and apologize for the various evil karmas committed throughout immeasurable kalpas.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* states:
"Although the nature of karma is empty, its retribution is not lost;
through the conditions of inversion, various grave offenses arise."
Shedding tears and weeping with grief, one should proclaim repentance aloud and think within the mind:
"I and all sentient beings, from the beginningless past..."
Constantly obstructed by the heavy transgressions of the three karmas and six sense faculties,
they do not see the Buddhas and do not know the essential way out.
Merely following the cycle of birth and death, they do not understand the wondrous principle.
Although I now know this, because I am the same as all sentient beings,
I am obstructed by all manner of grave offenses.
Now, before Avalokiteśvara and the Buddhas of the ten directions, [I confess].
For the sake of all sentient beings, I take refuge and repent.
I pray only that you will grant your protection so that all obstacles may be extinguished.
Having thus reflected, chant:
May all sentient beings within the dharma-realm— the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence—
universally vow to sever and eliminate the three obstacles.
Having finished chanting the "Homage and Repentance," one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and further reflects in the mind:
"From beginningless time until now, I and all sentient beings..."
Due to craving and false views, they internally conceive of a self and persons, while externally associating with evil friends;
they do not rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of another's merit,
but instead extensively commit all manner of transgressions through the three karmas.
Although the actual deeds were not extensive, his evil intentions pervaded everywhere;
they continued day and night without interruption,
as he concealed his faults and was unwilling to let others know them.
Having previously feared neither the evil realms nor the absence of shame and remorse,
and having repudiated cause and effect,
they now, on this day, possess deep faith in cause and effect.
Giving rise to profound shame and remorse, and engendering great fear,
they confess their transgressions openly, severing the continuity of their negative tendencies.
They resolve to attain bodhicitta, abandoning evil and cultivating goodness.
Diligently restrain the three karmas to reverse past grave transgressions; rejoice in even a hair’s breadth of merit performed by ordinary or noble beings;
and contemplate that the Buddhas of the ten directions possess great merit and wisdom, capable of rescuing and delivering myself and all sentient beings.
They have been led from the ocean of the two deaths to the shore of the three virtues.
Since beginningless time, they have remained ignorant of the fact that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, thereby extensively committing various evils.
Now, knowing emptiness and stillness as the means to seek Bodhi,
I extensively cultivate all manner of goodness for the sake of sentient beings and completely sever all evils; I pray only that Avalokiteśvara will behold me.
Having completed the visualization of gathering [beings] through compassion, chant:
"With a sincere heart, we repent,
Bhikṣu So-and-so and others."
Together with all sentient beings of the dharma-realm,
they manifest before them a single mind inherently endowed with the thousand dharmas;
all possess spiritual power and the clarity of wisdom, equal to the supreme mind of the Buddhas.
Below this, the consciousness of the dwelling-place (ālaya-vijñāna) has been stirred by beginningless darkness;
it obstructs this quiescent clarity, causing confusion in all encounters with phenomena and binding the mind through attachment whenever it is raised.
Within the dharma of equality, they give rise to the notions of self and other;
with craving and views as their basis and body and speech as their conditions,
there is no unwholesome deed they do not commit within the various realms of existence.
Committing the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes; slandering the Dharma and its practitioners;
violating the precepts, breaking the fasts, destroying stupas, and ruining monasteries;
stealing the property of the Saṃgha, and defiling pure celibacy.
To defraud or damage the food, drink, or property of the Sangha’s permanent endowment is a transgression that cannot be absolved through repentance even if a thousand Buddhas appear in the world.
Such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless.
If one abandons this physical life, one will fall into the three miserable realms;
there, one will endure myriad sufferings, and furthermore, in this present life, various afflictions will burn together:
either malignant diseases will entwine the body, or external circumstances will press upon it.
Hindered from practicing and cultivating the dharmas of the Path,
one now encounters this Great Compassionate and Perfect Divine Mantra,
which can swiftly eliminate such karmic obstacles.
Therefore, on this day, I recite and uphold [this] with a sincere heart,
taking refuge in Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the Great Teachers of the ten directions.
Having resolved to attain Bodhicitta and practiced the rites of mantra and mudrā, I confess and reveal all my transgressions to all sentient beings;
I pray for repentance so that they may be utterly eliminated. May it be so.
May the Great Compassionate Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara,
with his thousand hands providing protection and his thousand eyes illuminating all,
cause all internal and external obstacles and conditions for us to be pacified and extinguished.
Having perfected the practices and vows for oneself and others,
one opens the fundamental vision and knowledge to subdue all demons and externalists;
through diligence of the three karmas, one cultivates the causes for the Pure Land.
Upon casting off this body, they will have no further rebirths;
they will certainly attain birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha and personally receive offerings from the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara.
Possessing all dhāraṇīs, they extensively deliver all classes of beings,
causing them all to emerge from the wheel of suffering and together reach the ground of wisdom.
Having finished the confession and the making of vows:
Having taken refuge and paid homage to the Triple Gem by performing one prostration,
one should next circumambulate according to the Dharma,
either three or seven times. When about to circumambulate:
First, one must correctly visualize this maṇḍala as being identical to the dharma-realm,
with the Triple Gem of the ten directions filling the void of space.
Then, turn the body in succession to circumambulate the Dharma seat.
The nature of mind of the Triple Gem in the ten directions is quiescent and extinguished;
its manifestations throughout the ten directions are like dreams.
